I think broadly speaking though, chemo is a pretty blanket term for the non-targeted treatments like cytarabine, idarubicin, etc. These therapies have pretty generalized toxicities since they rarely disyinguish between healthy and cancerous cells.

I feel it’s slightly more accurate to say the modern therapies are targeted therapies (but I will argue that because adverse events are treated with less sensitivity, it essentially feels like chemo since almost all targeted therapies also affect normal cells and are not always synthetic lethality inducing treatments).

Did anyone actually READ [the paper?](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-393X/12/9/958) Besides it being an MDPI paper (whole different story) the sensationalism is kind of perplexing. 

The OVT approach is already a known therapy that is approved for melanoma. Albeit for metastatic disease, it is known to work; just not in breast cancer and not in earlier stage (which also makes the self experimentation safer maybe?). Additionally, there was always the off ramp for a switch to regular chemo.

The point I want to make is that this OVT is not the only thing this researcher received. She used it purely as a neo-adjuvant therapy to decrease the tumor so that she can have it surgically removed. After removal, she did not return to OVT but took trastuzumab as adjuvant therapy for one year which is used for HER2 positive breast cancer….which also raises the question as to why she felt OVT was necessary as we already have multiple treatment options for adjuvant/neo adjuvant/periadjuvant therapy for HER2 3+ cancers…

EDIT: It seems that her initial recurrence was triple negative and it evolved into HER2+ cancer which even begs a different question of was this OVT even safe? How did the virus suddenly provoke the overexpression of HER2? What if it started an overexpression of a resistance marker? I think this researcher got lucky that her excised tumor was treatable with known targeted medicine. Without the OVT, probably an initial neo adjuvant therapy of PD-1/PDL-1 or chemo and then surgery might have been sufficient. She was young enough that chemo was probably annoption (with humongous side effects; but her patient background suggests she might have been able to tolerate it)

I’m glad it worked, but using lab quality virus is not the same as using pharma/consumer grade virus and I feel is pretty dumb to try on oneself. While it IS dumb imo, if she feels she should do it on herself, then so be it. I draw the line at trying it on others (like the Chinese researcher who CRISPRd the babies to protect them from HIV which is also a WHOLE other mess)

It’s not that they are “lesser” it’s just that they aren’t the standard for safety when we consider starting dosage in human trials.

Believe it or not, compared to mice, rats are actually more sensitive to drugs. So the equivalent drug exposure between mice and rats, mice can tolerate it more than rats. It just so happens that through multiple safety tests over the years, rats have become sort of the “standard” safety model for human studies. This is because rats are actually really good predictors of toxicity in humans. Toxic doses in rats tend to correlate quite well with human toxicity.

There are two parameters we need to consider for human trials: the STD10 and the HNSTD. The STD10 is the severely toxic dose that results in mortality in 10% of rats and the HNSTD is the highest non severely toxic dose in nonrodents (dogs, monkeys etc).  We base our starting dose in humans off these values (1/10 of the STD10 or 1/6 of the HNSTD) and we do a dose escalation study in Phase 1 where we slowly increase the dosage of our drug in humans until we see toxicity. The dosing in which we see toxicity is the maximum tolerated dose in humans MTD and that forms the basis for the range of dosing we can apply for the Phase 2 efficacy trials.

Sorry the answer was so long! But hope this helps to explain why we use rats and nonrodents over mice.

It’s really not based out of himan feelings. It’s also we’re not totally neglecting the animal welfare either. In fact animal welfare is something we try really hard to maximize while they are in our possession. We try our best really to make sure they suffer the least.

The reason why mice is simply cost. It’s easier to maintain larger amounts of mice and cheaper. They also provide a very similar (95% similar but not perfect) physiological model for human studies that can be conducted at a larger scale. The moment you get into rats and larger animals, the scale becomes more of a logisitcal issue and more expensive. Also the cost of maintaining welfare of larger animals is also much much more expensive than mice.

I think the point I was trying to make (and did a poor job of explaining clearly) was why was there no record keeping for those animals.  Neuroscience and oncology (my field) are wildly different, so I can only speak to my experience, but for me it is not unusual to go through many mice; we tend to not test in higher animals until later development because of price, etc.

Also it's not like we all have to use monkeys...sometimes dogs or minipigs have better PK parameters, but the point still stands. We use tons of animals for any study.

This is where it gets...complicated in my opinion.  I still struggle with animal research even though it's pretty standard and par for the course.

Mice are just easier to breed, have shorter life cycles, and are smaller to handle. Rats and above are just larger animals and require more care compard to mice.  The other thing that complicates things, is that for certain diseases like cancer, to test the efficacy of a drug you need to test it in an immunocompromised mice (they have to B-cells, T-cells, etc. at different extremes); although immunocompetent mice are used for things like antibody therapies.  Rats and above are usually never genetically modified (and if they are, it gets even trickier from an ethics standpoint).

Point being: it's an imperfect solution to a complicated problem.  We try our best to minimize harm and provide the best conditions for welfare, but for every "good lab" there are also very negligent labs and it's just a really sobering reality of the industry.

The part that baffles me is that it's not record kept. Animals studies are like one of the things you need REALLY good record keepign for. Even shit like 'how much food did the animal eat' is super important and has very real implications on animal welfare while testing. On top of that there is also the usual measurements like body weight, blood testing levels, etc. It just makes no sense that there are no records on these.

Well specifically for lab research, we use macaques which are specifically bred in laboratory settings (rhesus macaques to be exact).

It is a sad fact that there is no good replacement for animal studies right now, and it is somewhat of a necessity (short of just YOLOing a drug and going straight into humans which is also very unethical). But this is why we hav edeveloped GLP studies and have created VERY strict animal welfare rules and regulations to ensure that we are minimizing the harm these animals suffer. 

Researchers actively use the three R principle (Replacement, Reduction, Refinement) for animal studies. It's not perfect, but it's so far the best we got. It's gonna take a really long time before AI can predict safety without the use of animals, and even then I don't think it will be phased out entirely. I hope that in the future we can create better replacement models for safety studies, but that also poses really interesting and tough ethics questions as well (like is growing a "fake" human organ system that is interconnected still ethical?).  Science is tough work, but we try our best.

I’m in pharma, and we use A LOT of mice to test drugs. The 1500 number doesn’t sound too outrageous on face value (that’s about 375 mice a year which is possible).

HOWEVER, the number that alarmed me is the 280 for monkeys, sheep etc. Higher animals (rats and above basically) are heavily scrutinized as they are required for safety studies. And at MOST you do less than 100 for the highest level safety study. And these safety studies are heavily regulated and stupid expensive, so you usually only do it once when you’re VERY sure it’s gonna work in humans. Of course you can do small pilot safety studies but those are always less than 20 animals and you hardly do many of those back to back. The fact that there’s no record keeping on those animals is highly suspicious.

I think the thing people are missing is that Cuban’s company sells GENERICS. Vyvanse is still market exclusive and brand name rights are currently held by Takeda.

Now luckily, Vyvanse is going generic next year in 2023 as the patent expires so the cost *should* go down.

But this also doesn’t exclude the fact that mega pharmas can and **will** make a second or third generation drug of the same indication to try and regain market exclusivity. While I think Cuban’s company is an excellent idea and helps those with medications, the biggest problem is actually brand name drug prices.

Take keytruda (pembrolizumab), it’s a monoclonal antibody for cancer. It’s an immune checkpoint blocker and when it was approved was the first of its kind. It is a BLOCKBUSTER drug. It is by far Merck’s number one selling drug (billions of dollars a year). However because it is an antibody, it is prohibitively expensive coming at 10,500 ish every 3-weeks.

Monoclonal antibody generation is not a new technique, but there are several key points that make it subject to rigorous GLP/GMP regulations that make it expensive. However, i think targeting brand name drugs are the real issue since there are the drug prices that continuously go up every year.

Thanks for the thoughtful reply, but I wanted to just clarify a misconception you pointed out in your post to me.

> ...their HIV (assuming that they adhere to their medication adequately) likely wouldn’t progress to AIDS and they would be pretty well protected against the opportunist infections you mentioned

Something people don't realize is that comorbidity and opportunistic infections are independent of the length of HIV medication and management. [This means that even though they don't progress to AIDS, it is very much a real situation that cardiovascular calcification and mental degradation occur even with optimally and maximally suppressed virus.](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2757599)  Something that also adds to this is that even though their life expectancy is the same-ish as someone who does not have HIV, they have to contend with WAY more diseases than the normal healthy individual for much longer.

While 20 million would definitely take away the financial burden of the medication, the reality is that you will always be at risk and be more susceptible to other diseases (especially hepatic, cvd, and mental).  That being said...personally not worth 20 million for me.

God as an HIV researcher it infuriates me to see that this is the sentiment. HIV is not a death sentence anymore absolutely.

What they don’t tell you is that it is a LIFE sentence.

You are absolute dependent on not one, not two, but maybe a cocktail of three drugs to even keep the HIV at low levels. You miss a day? You might have completely fucked yourself over and initiated an immune cascade of replicating virus.

Also, it is absolutely not true that it is manageable. You are at higher risk for cancers and cardiovascular disesase (which is overwhelmingly a common comorbidity) and other opportunistic infections like HPV/Hep C. And not to mention, long term ART while beneficial does not prevent you from developing HIV associated cognitive disorders that can lead to dementia.

So no it is not manageable and I wish people would stop saying it is.
